Kaarigar Works: The Supply That Would Not Stay

Sixteen points of professional retention have gone somewhere between January and July. Four people can each prove it went somewhere different.

1. Wednesday night, Gurugram

At 11:40 pm on 14 October 2026, Ira Bhattacharya, Chief Product Officer of Kaarigar Works, was still in the Udyog Vihar office with two laptops open and the air conditioning already switched off for the night. The board call was at 9:30 the next morning. The pre-read she had circulated on Monday contained one chart that nobody had commented on and one sentence that everybody had: 90-day professional retention has fallen from 54 percent for the January onboarding cohort to 38 percent for the July cohort.

Retention of professionals — electricians, plumbers, carpenters, AC technicians — was not a vanity metric at Kaarigar. Every pro who stopped taking jobs had cost between ₹2,100 and ₹6,400 to recruit, verify, background-check and train, and had absorbed a ₹1,800 uniform-and-tools kit. Diwali fell on 8 November. Kaarigar's demand forecast for the festival fortnight assumed 96,000 active professionals across 41 cities. On 14 October the number was 78,400 and had been flat for five weeks, even though 1.04 lakh pros had been onboarded since April.

The gap between those two numbers was the whole problem. Kaarigar was recruiting professionals faster than it ever had and holding fewer of them than it ever had, and the finance team's model said that at a 38 percent ninety-day rate the company would spend roughly ₹26 crore between October and January simply replacing the people it had already paid to recruit.

On one laptop was Vaishnavi Rangarajan's analysis from Toronto, which said the fall was mostly a question of who Kaarigar had recruited. On the other was a WhatsApp voice note from Rekha Salunkhe in Pune, twelve minutes long, which said the pros were leaving because there were not enough jobs to go round. Ira had read both three times. They could not both be the main story, and she could not yet prove that either of them was.

2. How Kaarigar got here

Kaarigar Works was founded in Gurugram in 2019 by Suresh Iyengar, a former Flipkart category head, and two engineers from Pune. The proposition was ordinary and the execution was not: a consumer app for booking home repair and maintenance, and a professional app that handled job allocation, navigation, spare-parts ordering, digital payment collection through UPI and weekly settlement. It competed with Urban Company in the metros, with NoBroker's services arm in Bengaluru and Mumbai, and everywhere with the neighbourhood electrician whose number was written on a sticker inside the meter cupboard.

The decision that shaped everything came in 2023. Individual recruitment of professionals was slow — roughly 40 pros per city per month — and Suresh chose instead to sign partner agencies: small contractors who already employed ten to sixty technicians and would bring them onto the platform in a batch. Supply growth went from 40 a month per city to 400. The price was structural. Under the partner agreements, the account belonged to the agency, not the technician; agencies bulk-uploaded phone numbers and Aadhaar-verified identity documents on their workers' behalf; and Kaarigar contractually waived any per-pro onboarding fee in exchange for volume commitments. Three years later, Kaarigar could not always tell whether a "churned" professional had left the platform or had simply been reassigned by his agency to another site under a different number. The 2023 decision bought the company its scale and mortgaged its ability to answer the question Ira now had to answer.

A second consequence of the 2023 decision was cultural. Agency-sourced technicians never signed up for Kaarigar; they were enrolled into it by an employer, and the company's onboarding flow, written for a self-selecting electrician who had downloaded the app after seeing a hoarding, had never been redesigned for a man handed a phone at a depot in Bhubaneswar and told to complete his profile before Monday. Everyone at Kaarigar knew this. Nobody had ever been able to say how much it mattered, because agency pros and organic pros had never differed much in the numbers until this year.

3. The market

Indian home services in 2026 was a market with real money and unreliable margins. Urban Company had established the category and the consumer price expectation. ONDC had opened a services catalogue that let small local providers list without a platform, and Kaarigar had joined the pilot in February 2026, which brought in a thin, price-sensitive stream of demand. Quick-commerce players had trained consumers to expect arrival within an hour, a standard no home-repair network could meet economically. Regulation pressed from two sides: the DPDP Act made the bulk upload of workers' identity documents by partner agencies a question the legal team had opened a file on and not closed, and the GST registration threshold shaped whether a pro could be paid as an individual or had to route earnings through his agency.

Demand, meanwhile, had grown but not evenly. Consumer bookings rose 34 percent year on year in the metros and 61 percent in the four newest tier-2 cities — impressive until set beside a tenfold increase in professionals in those same four cities. Kaarigar's consumer marketing budget had been cut in April to fund the supply push, on the reasoning, minuted at the time and not revisited since, that supply was the binding constraint.

Kaarigar's exposure was not only Indian. In March 2026 it had signed Al Jazi Facilities Management LLC, a Dubai contractor with 2,400 maintenance technicians across commercial towers, to a ₹11.6 crore annual licence for a white-labelled enterprise version of the professional app. The deal had been the centrepiece of the Series C: ₹380 crore raised in January, led by Kanchan Growth Partners, on a story about a marketplace that could also sell software.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In February the board set a supply target of 1.2 lakh new professionals before Diwali. Prateek Sabharwal's growth team met it through four channels at once: more partner agencies, particularly in Indore, Coimbatore, Lucknow and Bhubaneswar; vernacular performance marketing on Meta and YouTube; a referral bonus of ₹1,200 per successful pro; and, from May, a tool-purchase loan of up to ₹40,000 offered with Madhupur Finserve, an RBI-registered NBFC, which drew a noticeably different applicant.

In June, Jonas Ritter's team in Berlin shipped a redesigned job-acceptance flow intended to reduce the time a pro spent deciding whether to take a job. At the time it was believed to be a pure interface improvement. Two things about it were learned later: the Bengaluru team, implementing it, had also moved the event that the data pipeline treated as a professional's first activation from first job completed to first job accepted; and the redesign shipped with a default job radius of 12 km for new pros, up from 5 km, which nobody had listed in the release notes.

In August the allocation algorithm was changed to weight a professional's historical response rate more heavily, on the reasonable ground that customers hated waiting. New professionals, having no response history, were assigned a neutral prior that in practice placed them behind established pros in the queue. Ira had approved the change herself in a one-line message on a Thursday evening.

What was believed in June was that the company had a scaling problem of a familiar kind: more pros, thinner training, slightly worse quality, fixable with better onboarding content. What was believed in August was that the July cohort was simply immature and would look better once its ninety days closed. That belief was testable and was not tested; when the July cohort's window did close on 29 September, its rate was 38 percent and it did not move.

By September the retention fall was visible. Vaishnavi's first decomposition, delivered on 22 September, cut the cohorts by acquisition channel and concluded that most of the movement was compositional. On 6 October Rekha Salunkhe sent city operations data suggesting that jobs available per active professional per week had fallen in every city and every channel. On 11 October, Vaishnavi noticed the June activation-definition change while rebuilding her pipeline, and wrote to Ira that Exhibit 3 "may be comparing two different things." She has not yet redone the work.

5. The people

Ira Bhattacharya, CPO, Gurugram. Owns the board slide and the product roadmap. She believes the honest answer is that nobody knows yet, and she is not sure a board will accept that. She has not told anyone that the August allocation change was hers.

Suresh Iyengar, co-founder and CEO, Gurugram. His position: the product has not regressed, the mix has changed, and Kaarigar should hold its nerve through Diwali. Series D conversations begin in January. He has not mentioned that the Series C term sheet carries a ratchet tied to supply-growth milestones measured on 31 December.

Prateek Sabharwal, VP Supply Growth, Bengaluru. His position: retention among agency-sourced pros looks bad only because agencies rotate workers, which is an artefact, not a loss. His OKR is the 1.2 lakh number. He has not volunteered that three agencies account for 40 percent of new supply, or that one of them is run by a former colleague.

Vaishnavi Rangarajan, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto. Her position: decompose before deciding, and do not act on Exhibit 3 until the definition break is repaired. She has not said that her rebuilt pipeline backfills activation events for pre-June cohorts using an inferred rule, so she cannot yet state which direction the bias runs.

Jonas Ritter, Principal Designer, Berlin. His position: the June redesign improved every measured interface metric and should not be blamed. He has not mentioned the radius default, which he learned about last week.

Sharanya Pillai, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Owns Al Jazi. Her position: enterprise technician activity is stable, so this is a marketplace problem and engineering should stay on the Dubai SLA work due in December. She has not said that Al Jazi's activity figure comes from Al Jazi's own HR system and has never been reconciled with Kaarigar's.

Michael Doran, Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey. His position: the future is enterprise licensing, and the marketplace should be stabilised, not expanded. He quotes Kaarigar's marketplace retention numbers in every enterprise pitch as proof of product quality, which he has not mentioned to Ira.

Rekha Salunkhe, City Operations Manager, Pune. Her position: pros leave when they do not get six jobs in their first fortnight, and supply has outrun demand in the new cities. She has not said that her team has been manually re-routing jobs to retain pros they judge worth keeping.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the foundation of the compositional reading. Every source retains worse than in January, but the two weakest sources also grew: the loan-linked channel from a tenth to a seventh of intake, and partner agencies from 40 to 49 percent, while organic halved its share. Exhibit 2 attempts to separate the two forces, and does so twice.

7. Voices

"Agencies rotate people between sites. Half of what the warehouse calls churn is a man who changed his SIM. We are measuring our own paperwork."Prateek Sabharwal, supply review, 29 September
"I can give you a number for mix. I cannot give you a number I would defend, because the activation field changed underneath me in June and I found out three days ago. If we present Split A tomorrow we are presenting the friendliest of three answers without saying the other two exist."Vaishnavi Rangarajan, email to Ira, 13 October, 07:12 IST
"Sir, work is not coming. In Indore I did nine jobs in September. Last year in Pune I was doing ten a week. The app is fine. There is no work in the app."Transcript, pro support call, Indore, 2 October (translated from Hindi)
"Every interface metric improved. Time to accept fell 41 percent. If the pros are unhappy it is not because of the screen."Jonas Ritter, product review, Berlin, 6 October
"Please do not pull the Bengaluru squads onto marketplace firefighting. Al Jazi's SLA review is 31 December and that is ₹11.6 crore of the renewal."Sharanya Pillai, Slack, 13 October
"Two of my best pros in Kothrud told me they are keeping the Kaarigar app for the weekday jobs and taking their own customers on weekends. They have not churned. They have just stopped needing us for half their income. I do not know which column that is in your dashboard."Rekha Salunkhe, voice note to Ira, 13 October
"We told Kanchan we would be at 96,000 active pros for Diwali. I would rather explain a soft retention number than a missed supply number."Suresh Iyengar, to Ira, corridor conversation, 14 October

8. The options as Ira sees them

Option A — cut the weak sources. Stop the Madhupur loan-linked channel and pause new partner-agency signings, on the argument that Kaarigar is buying supply that does not stay. This raises blended retention almost immediately, by arithmetic rather than by improvement, and costs roughly 22,000 of the remaining Diwali intake. The partner agreements carry 90-day termination notice, so the pause is slower than it sounds.

Option B — guarantee early work. Reserve a floor of jobs for professionals in their first fortnight, reversing the August allocation weighting for new pros and, where demand is thin, subsidising the difference. Rekha estimates six guaranteed jobs per new pro across the Diwali quarter at a subsidy cost near ₹9 crore. It treats the symptom Rekha sees and the symptom Exhibit 4 shows, and it would slightly worsen customer wait times during the peak.

Option C — report and continue. Present retention by source, state that no source's product experience has collapsed, keep the supply engine running to Diwali and revisit in January. Costs nothing, fixes nothing, and requires Ira to present Split A without the two splits that are less flattering.

Option D — rebuild the measurement first. Repair the activation definition, reconcile the two warehouses, and decompose within city-month cohorts rather than by acquisition source, which is the only cut that would separate a demand-density effect from a supply-quality effect. It takes three weeks Ira does not have and produces, on 5 November, an answer about a Diwali that will already have started.

A fifth possibility had been raised once, by Michael Doran on a Tuesday call, and dismissed in four minutes: stop growing marketplace supply altogether, hold the network at its current size through Diwali, and redirect the remaining Series C into the enterprise product that Al Jazi had proved a market for. It would fail the 31 December supply milestone outright. Michael had not raised it again.

Ira had written the four options on the whiteboard on Monday. On Wednesday night she noticed something about the list that she had not noticed then: A, B and C all assume the question is which source of professionals is at fault. Exhibit 4 does not contain a source column at all.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board call is at 9:30 am on 15 October. Diwali demand begins to build on 28 October and peaks 6–9 November. Bengaluru engineering enters code freeze on 25 October; two squads are committed to the Al Jazi SLA work through December. The Series C ratchet is measured on 31 December on supply growth, not on retention. Partner-agency contracts require 90 days' notice. The legal team's open file on DPDP consent for agency-uploaded worker data has a review date in January. Kaarigar has ₹214 crore of the Series C unspent, and Suresh has said in two consecutive leadership meetings that he intends to enter the Series D conversation with the supply number intact.

Figure 1. The decision timeline. Two of the seven events were never instrumented against retention, and both fall inside the window the board is asking about.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, how much of the 16-point fall would you attribute to the change in who Kaarigar recruited? Which of the three splits would you present, and what obliges you to disclose the others?
  2. Exhibit 3 and Exhibit 4 come from different systems and imply different causes. What would you need to see before you believed either one?
  3. Exhibit 5 shows that the worst-retaining source is also the most profitable per active month. How should that change the reading of Exhibit 1 — and does it make "retention" the wrong headline metric for this decision?
  4. Prateek argues that agency churn is a measurement artefact of the 2023 partner model. If he is right, how much of Exhibit 1 survives? If he is wrong, how would you demonstrate it before Diwali?
  5. Ira approved the August allocation change and has not said so. What does she owe the board, and how does the disclosure change the credibility of each option she presents?
  6. What should Ira do on Monday morning, given that the answer will not be known until November — and what exactly would she say to the board at 9:30 tomorrow about a number she cannot yet decompose?

At ten past midnight Ira opened Exhibit 4 again and tried, for the fourth time, to work out whether a pro in Indore getting 4.3 jobs a week was a supply problem, a demand problem, an algorithm problem or a product problem, and whether the answer would be different if she had recruited him through an agency. The Al Jazi renewal note was still unread in the other window. The call was in nine hours.

The Bhavtaal Money Retention Question

A blended number has fallen sixteen points before Friday's board call. Is the product broken, or is the audience different?

1. Tuesday, Bengaluru

On the evening of 15 September 2026, Rohan Deshpande, Vice-President of Product at Bhavtaal Money, sat in the company's HSR Layout office in Bengaluru with three days left before Friday's board call. Bhavtaal's board — anchored by two Mumbai-based growth funds and one Singapore family office — had asked for one slide: why had Month-3 retention among new SIP (systematic investment plan) investors fallen from a steady 62 percent to 46 percent between the March and July starter cohorts? The board had also asked, in the same email, whether Bhavtaal's newest and most publicised growth channel — a corporate savings-benefit partnership with a large Dubai conglomerate — was working. Rohan suspected the two questions had the same answer, and that answer was not yet on any slide.

2. Bhavtaal Money

Founded in Pune in 2019, Bhavtaal Money let Indian retail investors start direct mutual-fund SIPs, trade stocks through a broking partner, and set savings goals from a single app, competing in the same crowded lane as Zerodha, Groww, INDmoney and Paytm Money. It operated under SEBI's investment-adviser and broking regulations and used NPCI's UPI Autopay to authorise recurring SIP debits, a detail that mattered more than most people at Bhavtaal usually noticed. By mid-2026 it had 2.4 million registered users and roughly 480,000 monthly active investors, earning revenue through broking commission and a paid tier, Bhavtaal Plus, that offered goal-tracking and tax-planning tools. Growth had historically come from organic search, personal-finance YouTube creators, and word-of-mouth referral — channels that were slow but produced investors who kept investing.

3. The situation

In March 2026, Bhavtaal signed a benefits partnership with Manaar Global Holdings, a Dubai-headquartered conglomerate with roughly 40,000 India-based and NRI-linked employees, to offer Bhavtaal Money as a salary-linked savings benefit. Around the same time, with a board-set target of 500,000 new SIP starters before Diwali, Bhavtaal's growth team ran an aggressive Instagram and Meta performance-marketing push alongside the Manaar rollout. Monthly SIP starters rose from roughly 60,000 to 140,000 by July. The board had celebrated the volume in June. By September, Priyanka Iyer, Bhavtaal's Toronto-based data scientist, had flagged that the July cohort's blended Month-3 retention — the share still making at least one SIP debit in their third month — had fallen to 46 percent, down from 62 percent for cohorts that started before the Manaar rollout. She had not yet said why, only that the timing lined up too closely with the new channels to be coincidence.

The global team saw the number differently depending on where they sat. From New Jersey, Brian Whitfield, who led growth for the North American and NRI corridor and had championed the Manaar deal as a signature story for Bhavtaal's upcoming Series D pitch, argued the dip was noise from a bigger, younger cohort still settling in. From Berlin, Lukas Bergmann, the product designer who had shipped a simplified Aadhaar-based e-KYC flow in June specifically to cut onboarding drop-off, worried privately that his redesign might be the actual cause, though the drop-off numbers he owned had, if anything, improved. From Singapore, Meera Krishnan, who managed the Manaar account for customer success, had been fielding a rising number of complaints from employees' family members — the actual users behind many of the new SIPs — who said the goal-based interface was confusing and that they had not entirely chosen to start investing in the first place.

4. The people

  • Rohan Deshpande, VP Product, Bengaluru — owns the Friday board slide and the decision of what, if anything, to fix before then.
  • Priyanka Iyer, Data Scientist, Toronto — built the cohort dashboards; insists on decomposing the number before anyone tells a story about it.
  • Brian Whitfield, Head of Growth, NRI Corridor, New Jersey — wants the Manaar partnership and paid-growth pace protected ahead of fundraising.
  • Lukas Bergmann, Lead Product Designer, Berlin — owns the June onboarding redesign and fears it will be blamed without evidence.
  • Meera Krishnan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore — manages the Manaar relationship and hears directly from confused, low-intent new investors.

5. The exhibits

Priyanka's first exhibit split the July cohort of 140,000 SIP starters into the same three channels used every quarter, and compared each channel's own Month-3 retention against March, before the Manaar rollout and the ad push had changed the mix.

ChannelMarch startersMarch M3 retentionJuly startersJuly M3 retention
Organic & referral42,000 (70%)68%42,000 (30%)68%
Paid, general12,000 (20%)44%42,000 (30%)44%
Manaar partnership6,000 (10%)52%56,000 (40%)30%
Blended60,00061.6%140,00045.6%

Exhibit 1 shows two things at once: organic and paid-general retention had not moved at all, and the Manaar channel had grown from a tenth of starters to two-fifths of them while its own retention fell from 52 to 30 percent. Exhibit 2 makes the same numbers visible as a bridge, separating what mix alone would have done from what actually happened.

Priyanka pushed one level further inside the Manaar segment alone, splitting its own retention into the share of new investors who confirmed their UPI Autopay mandate within seven days of enrolment ("activation") and, among those who did, the share still investing in month three. In March, 75 percent of the small Manaar cohort activated, and 69 percent of activated investors were still investing by month three: 0.75 × 0.69 ≈ 52 percent. In July, activation had fallen to 58 percent, and conditional retention among the activated had also slipped to about 52 percent: 0.58 × 0.52 ≈ 30 percent. The reason, Meera's team had already documented in support tickets: Manaar's HR system bulk-enrolled employees and eligible family members directly, and many of those accounts required an individual OTP-based bank confirmation that the bulk process could not complete on anyone's behalf — a real activation-side operational gap, sitting alongside a real, separate engagement-side gap among family members who had been auto-enrolled rather than having chosen to invest.

6. The options

Option A — Pause and renegotiate the Manaar bulk-enrollment design. Rohan could ask Manaar to move to opt-in enrolment, protecting Bhavtaal's retention quality and its broking-book economics. The upside is a cleaner metric and less regulatory exposure from a growing pool of dormant SIP mandates. The cost is real: a marquee enterprise partnership, publicised in the Series D narrative Brian was building, would shrink in scale, and Manaar's HR director, Yusuf Al Marzouqi, would need to be told the model is changing before it was fully proven to fail.

Option B — Fix the activation gap and keep the volume. Rohan's team could build a lightweight in-app nudge sequence that prompts newly bulk-enrolled Manaar users to complete their UPI mandate confirmation within forty-eight hours, targeting a return toward the 75 percent activation rate seen in March, while leaving the partnership and the ad push untouched. This is the cheapest, fastest, and most narrowly evidenced fix, costing the Pune engineering team roughly two weeks, but it may not close the smaller, intent-driven engagement gap among family members who never chose to invest on their own.

Option C — Reframe the board metric and buy time. Rohan could present Month-3 retention broken out by channel rather than blended, argue correctly that the core product has not regressed, and continue the current pace into the Diwali push while monitoring. This is honest and requires no immediate operational change, but it fixes nothing, risks looking like spin to a board that asked a direct question, and leaves a growing base of unconfirmed UPI mandates that SEBI or Bhavtaal's own auditors could reasonably ask about later.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2, how much of the 16-point drop is a mix problem, and how much is a within-segment problem? Show the arithmetic.
  2. What role does Manaar's bulk-enrollment design play in blurring "who signed up" from "what they did once enrolled"?
  3. Weigh Rohan's three options against what the decomposition can and cannot support. Which claims does the data back, and which would be overreach?
  4. What should Rohan tell the board on Friday, and what should he commit to fixing immediately versus monitoring over the next quarter?

8. A note for the learner

This case is a clean illustration of why a single retention number is dangerous currency in a board meeting. The 16-point fall looks, at first glance, like a product failure large enough to justify an engineering freeze. Decomposition shows that most of it, 7.2 of the 16 points, is arithmetic: Bhavtaal simply brought in more people through a channel that always retained worse than organic, and would have shown roughly this fall even if nothing else in the company had changed. The remaining 8.8 points sit inside one segment, and splitting that segment by activation and conditional engagement shows the fall there is not one problem but two overlapping ones — an operational onboarding gap that engineering can fix in weeks, and an intent gap that no onboarding fix will fully close, because many of these investors did not choose to be there.

A well-reasoned answer does not pick a single option and defend it as the only correct one; it sequences the three. The most defensible path is to fix the activation gap first (Option B), since it is cheap, has clear ownership in Pune, and is the one claim the data supports without ambiguity; to tell the board the truth in decomposed form rather than either alarming or reassuring headline (part of Option C, honestly used); and to treat the deeper question of whether bulk enrolment is the right long-term design for corporate-benefit partnerships (Option A) as a strategic decision for Rohan, Brian and the board to make together over the following quarter, once the cheap fix has run and the two effects can be told apart with less noise. Acting on Option A immediately, before the activation fix has even been tried, would risk giving up a partnership over a problem that a two-week engineering change might substantially solve.

Decomposing Retention Changes

Attributing a retention shift to mix, activation or engagement — and knowing when the attribution itself is the wrong instrument.

1. Two rooms, one number

On the morning of 4 September 2026, Devika Menon, Director of Product at Gulmohar Reads, a Mumbai subscription app for books and serialised fiction, had a slide with a single line on it: Day-30 retention for the July signup cohort was 31 percent, against 41 percent in February. Six months, ten points, roughly 2.4 lakh new readers over the period. The annual plan was due in eleven days and two proposals sat in front of the leadership team: rebuild the reading-streak system at a cost of about two engineer-quarters, or cut performance-marketing spend by a third and take the growth hit. Both proposals cited the same slide. Only one of them could be responding to what had actually happened.

A week later and 1,200 kilometres away, Arjun Vaidyanathan, general manager of Maapdand Systems, a Pune-headquartered vendor of factory inspection software sold to auto-component and appliance manufacturers, was preparing a quarterly business review. His problem looked nothing like Devika's and was structurally identical. Maapdand's seat-level retention — the share of named inspectors still logging an inspection in month six — had slipped from 74 to 66 percent across the accounts signed in the previous year. His head of customer success attributed it to a support-staffing gap. His head of sales, who had spent the year moving upmarket from twenty-seat plants to two-hundred-seat multi-plant groups, did not think the product had changed at all. Arjun had no way to referee the argument, because the two of them were not disagreeing about a fact. They were disagreeing about which population the number described.

The central claim is simple to state and hard to execute: an aggregate retention rate is a weighted average, and any change in a weighted average has at least two sources — the weights and the values — which no amount of staring at the aggregate will separate. The complications begin immediately after that sentence and do not stop.

2. The idea, and the quarrel behind it

Write the blended retention rate of a cohort as R = Σ wi ri, where i indexes segments of the cohort — acquisition channel, city tier, plan, device, industry — wi is each segment's share of signups and ri its own retention rate. Comparing two cohorts, period 0 and period 1, the identity is exact:

ΔR = Σ Δwi ri0  (mix)  +  Σ wi0 Δri  (behaviour)  +  Σ Δwi Δri  (interaction)

Decomposing retention changes means computing those terms, then splitting the behaviour term again inside whichever segment moved, into whether new users ever reached a first meaningful use (activation) and whether those who did kept coming back (conditional retention, or engagement). The second split is also an identity, since a segment's retention equals its activation rate times retention conditional on activation.

The technique was not invented by product managers. Its direct ancestor is demographic standardisation, used by nineteenth-century actuaries to compare mortality between towns with different age structures, formalised for two-factor cases by Evelyn Kitagawa in 1955 in a paper that is still the cleanest statement of the problem: the difference between two crude rates is the sum of a composition effect and a rate effect, and the split depends on the order in which you take them. Regional economists built the same arithmetic into shift-share analysis around 1960, splitting a region's employment growth into national trend, industry mix and local competitiveness. Labour economists, following Oaxaca and Blinder in 1973, used it on wage gaps and spent thirty years arguing about the residual. Prakash Das Gupta's 1993 monograph generalised the standardisation to many factors with an order-free, symmetric weighting. Growth teams absorbed the logic in the 2010s, when Mixpanel and Amplitude made cohort-by-channel slicing cheap, and largely absorbed it without the literature — which is why product teams still rediscover, as a surprise, that their decomposition changes when they reverse the order of the terms.

Three schools use the same arithmetic for different purposes, and the differences are worth stating as propositions each would and would not sign.

The accounting school treats the decomposition as bookkeeping. It will sign: the split is an identity, it is exact, and its purpose is to stop people attributing an aggregate movement to a cause before the arithmetic has been done. It will not sign: the mix term is the effect of the mix change. To this school the terms are descriptive, not causal, and a practitioner who says "mix caused seven points" has already overclaimed.

The causal school, descended from the econometric reweighting literature, regards composition as confounding to be removed rather than a component to be reported. It will sign: the quantity of interest is what would have happened to the same population under the new product, which is estimated by reweighting, matching or, better, a holdout experiment. It will not sign: a channel is a treatment. Channel is chosen by the firm and correlated with everything, so a channel-level rate difference is not the effect of the channel on anybody.

The heterogeneity school, associated with Andrew Ehrenberg's buyer-behaviour work and with Peter Fader and Bruce Hardie's shifted-beta-geometric model of contractual churn, argues that retention curves flatten mainly because high-propensity users survive and low-propensity users leave — sorting, not product decay. It will sign: observed segments are noisy proxies for a latent distribution of propensity, and most of what teams call "engagement decline" is the mechanical consequence of that distribution's shape. It will not sign: a fall in conditional retention among activated users is evidence that the product got worse for them, because a change in who activates changes the propensity mixture inside the activated group, with no behavioural change at all.

These are genuinely different positions, not emphases, and they lead to different work. Devika's two proposals map onto them almost exactly: the streak rebuild is the operational reading, the spend cut is the composition reading, and nobody in her building was arguing the heterogeneity position, which turned out to matter.

3. Mechanics, worked all the way through

Devika's analyst pulled the February and July cohorts split by acquisition channel, with retention measured identically at thirty days. Exhibit 1 is the raw material.

ChannelFeb signupsFeb shareFeb D30Jul signupsJul shareJul D30
Organic & app store48,00040%52%42,00021%50%
Creator partnerships30,00025%46%34,00017%45%
Paid social36,00030%26%104,00052%18%
Telco bundle6,0005%30%20,00010%28%
Blended120,000100%41.0%200,000100%31.0%

Exhibit 1. Gulmohar Reads, D30 retention by acquisition channel, February and July 2026 signup cohorts. Both cohorts observed for a full thirty days; July's window closed on 31 August.

Taking the terms in the order of the identity: the mix term holds February's rates fixed and moves the weights. Paid social gains 22 points of share at a 26 percent rate while organic loses 19 points at 52 percent; summing Δwi ri0 across the four channels gives −6.7 points. The behaviour term holds February's weights fixed and moves the rates: −2.0, −0.25, −2.4 and −0.1, summing to −4.75 points, of which paid social's eight-point fall supplies half. The interaction term, Σ Δwi Δri, comes to +1.45 points: paid social's rate fell in exactly the period its weight rose, and the product of two negatives with a positive weight change is arithmetically positive. The three sum to −10.0, the observed fall.

Figure 1. The three-term decomposition of Gulmohar's ten-point fall, in the Laspeyres ordering: mix first at old rates, behaviour second at old weights, interaction as residual. Reversing the order moves roughly 1.45 points between the first two bars.

Now the step that most teams never take. Reverse the order — hold July's weights and move the rates first — and the behaviour term becomes −6.2 points while the mix term becomes −3.8. Nothing about the world changed; only the counterfactual did. This is the index-number problem, and it is why Kitagawa's paper exists. The discipline that resolves it is to refuse both orderings and use the symmetric, order-free form, which is the two-player Shapley value of the same game: mix = Σ Δwi (ri0 + ri1)/2 and behaviour = Σ (wi0 + wi1)/2 × Δri. For Gulmohar that gives mix −5.97 and behaviour −4.03, summing exactly to −10 with no residual to explain away. The practical consequence is not cosmetic. Under the Laspeyres reading, mix is 67 percent of the problem; under the reversed reading, 38 percent; under the symmetric reading, 60 percent. A leadership team deciding whether to cut ad spend is choosing between those framings whether or not anyone tells them so.

The second split runs inside paid social, whose own rate fell from 26 to 18 percent. Retention equals activation times conditional retention, where Gulmohar defined activation as finishing one chapter within forty-eight hours. Activation fell from 60 to 45 percent; conditional retention from 43.3 to 40.0 percent. Because the relationship is multiplicative, the clean way to apportion is in logarithms: ln(0.18) − ln(0.26) = −0.368, of which ln(0.45) − ln(0.60) = −0.288 is activation and −0.080 is conditional retention. Activation is 78 percent of the segment's own deterioration. In points of the blended number, paid social's behaviour contributed about −2.9 on the symmetric weighting, of which roughly −2.3 is activation.

Two further steps separate a careful analyst from a fast one. First, significance. Paid social's July cohort had 104,000 signups, so the standard error on an 18 percent rate is √(0.18 × 0.82 / 104,000) = 0.12 points; February's is 0.23 points. An eight-point move is not noise. But the telco bundle's 6,000-signup February cohort carries a standard error of 0.6 points, so its two-point move is inside the range where a team should say nothing. Teams routinely narrate all four rows with equal confidence. Second, censoring. If July's cohort had been measured on 20 August, its thirty-day window would be incomplete for late-July signups and its rate mechanically depressed — the single most common source of a fake retention decline, and the first thing to check before any decomposition is run.

4. When the decomposition applies, and when it misleads

The technique carries four conditions, each of which can be stated as a testable claim rather than a caveat.

The segmentation must be fixed before the data is seen, and must be stable in meaning across both periods. Devika chose channel in advance because channel was what her company had deliberately changed. Had she cut by city tier first, she would have found a smaller, real-looking effect and stopped. For Arjun the honest cut was plant size, because that is what his sales motion moved; cutting Maapdand's seats by user role would have described the same shift in the vocabulary of a different department.

The segments must partition the cohort and must not themselves be outcomes. Splitting by "users who enabled notifications" fails this test: notification opt-in is a consequence of engagement, so the decomposition would attribute retention to itself.

Both cohorts must have equal observation windows, equal metric definitions and comparable calendar exposure. Gulmohar's July cohort spent its first thirty days in the monsoon slack season; February's spanned an exam-results fortnight when reading time collapses. Arjun's six-month seat window straddled a plant shutdown for Diwali in one cohort and not the other. Neither is a product effect and both land in the behaviour term.

The segments must be numerous enough to sustain inference and few enough to interpret. Four to eight is the working range; forty campaign IDs produce noise dressed as insight.

Where it is actively misleading is more interesting. If the mix change and the behaviour change have a common cause, the decomposition will report them as separate and the reader will treat them as independent. When Gulmohar's paid-social spend tripled, the ad platform's optimiser moved down the audience quality curve within the channel; the falling within-channel rate is not a product regression but a continuation of the same mix effect, invisible because it happened underneath the segment label rather than between segments. Similarly, if the product change caused the mix change — a pricing test that repels one kind of user — the composition term is an effect of the product, and reporting it as "not our problem" is precisely wrong.

5. Hard edges

Two-sided marketplaces break the unit of analysis. Retention of a host or a driver depends on demand density, which depends on the number of hosts; cohorts are not independent, and a decomposition of supplier retention by acquisition channel will attribute to channel what is really a local equilibrium. The competent move is to decompose within a city-month, where density is roughly common, and to accept that the cross-city aggregate cannot be decomposed cleanly at all.

Multi-product firms face a definitional problem before an analytical one: retention of what? A user who stops using the feature they signed up for and starts using another is retained at the account level and churned at the product level, and the two decompositions can point in opposite directions. Mature companies resolve this by fixing the denominator to the entry product for the first ninety days and only then switching to account-level, but few say so in writing, and almost none apply it consistently across dashboards.

Hardware plus software makes the mix term physical. Mandara Wearables, a fitness-band maker, found app retention falling as retail distribution grew relative to direct sales; the decomposition correctly isolated the channel, but the underlying driver was that retail buyers received units with older firmware, so what looked like a mix effect was a mix effect with an operational cause attached, and fixing the ad spend would have done nothing.

AI-native products break comparability itself. At Lipika AI, a document-extraction tool, the model was upgraded twice between the two cohorts being compared. The February cohort and the July cohort did not use the same product, so the "behaviour" term contains an unmeasured product change, and the usual instinct — treat the model version as another segment dimension — fails because version is perfectly collinear with calendar time. What mature teams do is hold a small random slice of new users on the previous model version for a fixed window; what they say they do is decompose by prompt category.

Regulated products add a term nobody wants. In lending and broking, a KYC rule change alters who can activate, not who signs up, so the effect lands in activation and looks like product failure. At the organisational seam, this is where the decomposition usually dies: marketing owns mix, product owns activation, and the analytics team owns the arithmetic, so the term that gets investigated is the one whose owner is weakest in the room.

6. What separates an expert

The expert distrusts a clean answer. When a single segment explains eighty percent of a move, the tell is that the segment also changed size sharply. Coincident weight and rate movement in the same segment is usually one cause showing up twice, not two findings. The obvious reading — "we found it" — is wrong because the decomposition cannot distinguish a channel that got worse from a channel that was expanded into worse inventory.

The expert checks the denominator before the numerator. The tell is a retention fall that begins exactly when a signup definition, a bot filter or a tracking SDK changed. Adding previously excluded low-intent signups lowers retention without any user behaving differently. The obvious reading is that quality fell; in fact measurement widened.

The expert treats activation as a mediator, not a control. The tell is an analyst saying "controlling for activation, retention is flat." Activation sits downstream of whatever changed, so conditioning on it answers the direct-effect question and hides the total effect. Worse, conditioning on a post-signup outcome is a collider: comparing conditional retention across periods compares differently selected survivor populations, which is the heterogeneity school's central objection and is usually dismissed too quickly.

The expert knows the interaction term is not a rounding error. The tell is a deck where mix and behaviour sum to the total exactly with no residual mentioned, when the segments moved a lot. Either a symmetric method was used — in which case say so — or one ordering was silently chosen. The obvious reading, that the numbers simply add up, is wrong: they add up because someone made a choice.

The expert separates payment retention from usage retention. In subscription products the two can move in opposite directions for a quarter, because an annual plan holds the payment while usage decays. The tell is a flat revenue-retention line above a falling engagement line. The obvious reading — retention is fine — mistakes a contractual lag for a health signal, and the correction arrives at renewal.

The expert recognises a lifecycle artefact. If a fast-growing cohort mixes more first-week users into any period-based measure, blended retention falls without any cohort's curve changing. The tell is that a cohort-locked view is flat while the calendar view falls. The obvious reading is decline; the reality is growth arithmetic, and it reverses when growth slows — which means it will mislead in both directions.

The expert asks which term is actionable before asking which is largest. A six-point mix effect is not a bigger problem than a four-point activation effect if the mix change was a deliberate, funded strategy with a known payback. The tell is a room debating a number nobody has the authority to move. The obvious reading is that size determines priority; in practice, the ratio of effect to controllable lever does.

The expert holds the sample sizes in view. The tell is a decomposition with a segment whose cohort is under a few thousand users carrying a confident narrative. Small segments swing widely; three points on 2,000 users is barely a signal. The obvious reading treats all rows as equally informative because they are equally formatted.

The expert looks for the reversal. Simpson's paradox is not exotic here: every segment's retention can improve while the blended number falls. The tell is a behaviour term positive and a mix term larger and negative. The obvious reading — "retention is down, something broke" — is exactly backwards, and the correct answer to a board is uncomfortable: the product improved and we sold it to a harder audience on purpose.

The expert distinguishes a decomposition from an experiment. Decomposition narrows the hypothesis space; it does not test anything. The tell is a roadmap item justified solely by a decomposition. The obvious reading is that the arithmetic identified a cause. It identified a location, which is a different and lesser thing, and the cost of confusing them is a funded quarter aimed at a coincidence.

7. How it changes with product type and stage

In consumer products, cohorts are large enough for confident inference and channel mix moves as fast as ad spend, so mix effects dominate and the decomposition is run weekly. In B2B and enterprise the unit question comes first: seat retention, account retention and revenue retention decompose differently, and the meaningful segments are firmographic — size band, industry, implementation partner. Arjun's cohorts were fifty accounts, not fifty thousand users, so no segment-level rate was statistically distinguishable; his honest version of the exercise was a structured review of every churned account against a fixed taxonomy, which is decomposition by census rather than by sampling, and is often better.

Platforms and marketplaces, as noted, are the case where the technique most often produces confident nonsense, because the segments interact. Hardware businesses have slow, lumpy mix shifts tied to distribution deals, so the same analysis run quarterly rather than weekly is right. In AI products the pace of model change makes period-over-period cohorts non-comparable in a way that is genuinely unsolved; teams are honest when they say the behaviour term at this company includes a product they cannot hold constant.

By stage, the difference is real but narrower than people claim. Pre-product-market-fit, cohorts are too small and definitions too unstable for anything but the crudest cut, and time is better spent on qualitative exit interviews. At scale, mix effects grow because the firm buys more of its growth. The claim that early-stage teams should not do this at all is overstated: the discipline of asking "who came in?" before "what broke?" costs nothing and survives any sample size.

8. Three worked cases, one of them a failure

Gulmohar Reads. The symmetric decomposition gave mix −5.97, behaviour −4.03, of which paid social's activation collapse was roughly −2.3. Investigation found that a June release had moved the first-chapter screen behind a plan-selection interstitial shown only to users arriving from ad links. Fixing it cost three engineer-weeks and recovered paid social's activation from 45 to 57 percent within six weeks — worth about 2.0 points of blended D30, and nothing at all of the 5.97 mix points.

Maapdand Systems. With fifty accounts, Arjun abandoned rates and counted. Of eleven accounts with falling seat activity, eight were multi-plant groups where the pilot plant had gone live and the second and third plants never started, and three were small accounts with genuine product complaints. Segment share of large accounts had risen from 20 to 55 percent of new logos. The mix reading was correct; the fix was not a product fix but a change to the implementation contract, staging rollouts plant by plant with a named customer-success owner per site. Nothing in the product roadmap changed.

Haveli Stays — where the method failed. This homestay marketplace watched host 90-day retention fall from 58 to 44 percent over two quarters. The decomposition by host-acquisition channel produced a satisfying answer: a broker-referral channel had grown from 8 to 31 percent of new hosts and retained at 29 percent. The team cut broker referrals, and over the next quarter retention fell again, to 41. The decomposition had been arithmetically correct and causally empty. The true driver was a search-ranking change in March that had pushed new listings below a review-count threshold, so that hosts in every channel received their first booking later; broker-sourced hosts were simply the least patient. The recovery took two months: re-running the analysis with cohorts defined by listing-live date within a single city, using days-to-first-booking as the activation measure, showed the break clearly. The wasted quarter cost roughly ₹1.8 crore in host-acquisition spend redirected away from a channel that was not the problem, and the broker channel, once restored with a first-booking guarantee, retained at 47 percent.

Figure 2. Haveli Stays. Every channel's curve shifted down between quarters, including the one the team never suspected. A parallel move across all segments is the signature of a common cause upstream of the segmentation, and it is the pattern a mix decomposition is least equipped to see.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The first is stopping at mix. The warning sign is a deck that ends with a channel table. The diagnostic question is: within the channel that moved, did activation or conditional retention move? Caught late, the cost is a marketing budget cut that leaves a product defect shipping to every remaining channel.

The second is the immature cohort. The warning sign is that the most recent cohort is always the worst. The diagnostic question is whether every cohort in the comparison has completed the full observation window. Caught late, a team spends a sprint fixing a calendar.

The third is definition drift. The warning sign is a step change in a metric on a release date. The diagnostic question is what changed in instrumentation, bot filtering or the signup definition that week. Caught late, the correction arrives after a public commitment to a number.

The fourth is segment shopping. The warning sign is an analysis that tried six dimensions and reports one. The diagnostic question is which dimension was named before the data was pulled. Caught late, the organisation loses trust in the analytics function, which is expensive and slow to rebuild.

The fifth is treating the decomposition as the finding. The warning sign is a roadmap commitment with no experiment behind it. The diagnostic question is what test would distinguish this explanation from its nearest rival. Caught late — as at Haveli Stays — the cost is a full quarter and a channel relationship.

10. Where experts disagree

The first live disagreement is whether mix effects should be reported to boards at all. One camp argues that a blended retention number that mixes strategy changes with product changes is simply a badly constructed metric, and that segment-level retention with explicit weights should replace it everywhere. Their evidence is the frequency with which blended numbers cause misdirected investment. The opposing camp argues that blended retention is the only number that reflects the business the company actually has — a firm that buys worse users is a worse business, whatever its per-channel rates — and that segment-level reporting invites managers to explain away real deterioration. This position would be wrong if channel mix were genuinely temporary and reversible; it is right in proportion to how sticky the acquisition strategy is.

The second concerns the heterogeneity objection. The Fader–Hardie position is that decomposing into activation and conditional retention is contaminated by selection: change the activation rate and you change who is in the conditional group, so a fall in conditional retention may be pure sorting. The operational rejoinder is that this is true and mostly unimportant at the magnitudes teams observe, and that waiting for a latent-class model means shipping nothing. The heterogeneity camp would be wrong if activation gates were largely mechanical — an OTP, a permission prompt — since those select weakly on propensity. They are plainly right when activation is an effortful milestone that only motivated users reach.

The third is methodological and quieter: whether to use the symmetric Shapley-style split or to report one ordering with the residual visible. The symmetry camp values a unique, order-free answer with no unexplained term. The transparency camp answers that a large interaction term is itself the most useful finding — it says the weight and rate moves are entangled — and that averaging it away destroys information. Both are defensible; what is not defensible is silence about which was used.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this differs in three visible ways. They ask "compared to which cohort, measured over what window?" before they look at the number, and they refuse to discuss it until both are fixed. They name the segmentation dimension and the reason for it before the query runs, and they write the reason down, so that the analysis can be wrong rather than merely unfalsifiable. And they treat the output as a shortlist of hypotheses with an explicit next test attached to each, rather than as an explanation — which is why, when a mix effect explains sixty percent of a fall, they can tell a board that the product is fine, the strategy is expensive, and the remaining four points are the only part of this that engineering should touch.

12. The decisions

Devika took the symmetric decomposition to the annual plan with three lines: six points of the ten are the price of an acquisition strategy the board approved; three come from a June interstitial that ships only to ad traffic; one is unexplained. She funded three engineer-weeks, not two quarters, and asked the growth team for a paid-social payback model rather than a spend cut, on the argument that the mix question is a finance question wearing a product costume. Arjun did not decompose at all in the statistical sense. With fifty accounts he ran a census of churn reasons, found the multi-plant rollout gap, and changed the implementation contract — then instrumented plant-level activation so that next year the question could be answered properly.

Three questions for discussion. First: if Gulmohar's paid-social channel is unprofitable at its current retention, is the mix effect a product failure, a marketing failure, or a pricing failure, and who should own it? Second: Maapdand has fifty accounts and no statistical power — at what sample size should Arjun switch from census to decomposition, and what would he lose in the transition? Third: at Haveli Stays, what single check, run before the channel analysis, would have caught the common-cause shift, and why do experienced teams so rarely run it?

13. Going deeper

  1. Retention curves and the PMF signal — the shape a decomposition operates on; a flattening curve and a falling level are different diseases, and only one of them threatens the business model.
  2. Root cause analysis of a metric change — the general procedure this topic specialises; it supplies the discipline of ruling out instrumentation and seasonality before any segment cut.
  3. Constructing a funnel — decomposition needs a milestone to split on, and the funnel is where that milestone is defined and defended.
  4. Reading drop-off — once activation is identified as the moving term, drop-off analysis locates the specific step, which decomposition never does.
  5. Defining activation (the aha moment) — the single choice that determines whether the activation term means anything; a badly chosen milestone makes the entire second split noise.
  6. Cohort analysis — the data structure underneath everything here, including the cohort-versus-calendar distinction that causes the lifecycle artefact.
  7. Stickiness and natural frequency — tells you whether a thirty-day window is the right measurement period at all, which decomposition assumes rather than establishes.
  8. Feature adoption analysis — the natural next cut once the engagement term is implicated, moving from who and whether to what inside the product changed.

Decomposing Retention Changes

Did retention drop because of who came in, or because of what they did once they arrived?

1. A number that frightened the wrong people

On the first Monday of September 2026, Aditi Kulkarni, senior growth PM at Manthan Fitness, a Bengaluru-based subscription workout app competing for the same wallets as Cult.fit and a scatter of city-specific gym-booking apps, opened a dashboard she wished she hadn't. Month-2 retention — the share of a signup cohort still completing at least one paid check-in fifty to seventy days after joining — had fallen from 38 percent for the May cohort to 28 percent for the August cohort. Manthan's board met in nine days, and the CEO had already texted her: "Is the app getting worse?" The honest answer, Aditi suspected, was more interesting and more useful than either yes or no.

The stakes were concrete. Manthan had just closed a bridge round on the strength of its retention story, and the same August cohort was the one investors would ask about first. If Aditi told the board "the product regressed" and the true cause was who Manthan had recently chosen to advertise to, engineering would spend a quarter chasing a bug that did not exist. If she said "it's just marketing" and part of the drop was in fact a broken onboarding step, the company would keep bleeding new members while blaming an innocent ad campaign. She needed a way to open the number up before deciding what, if anything, to fix.

2. The idea, plainly

Retention-change decomposition is the practice of splitting an observed change in a retention rate between two cohorts, or between two periods, into the portion caused by a shift in who signed up (the mix of acquisition channels, cities or plans), the portion caused by a shift in whether new users ever reach a meaningful first-use milestone (activation), and the portion caused by a shift in how often already-activated users keep coming back (engagement). It exists because a single blended retention number answers "what happened" but is silent on "why," and that silence is expensive: two very different problems — a bad marketing channel and a broken product screen — can produce an identical drop in the headline metric.

The technique itself has no single inventor with a textbook citation; it is a specific application of an older statistical idea, standardisation or "shift-share" decomposition, used by demographers and labour economists since the mid-twentieth century to separate a change in an average (say, wages) into a compositional effect and a within-group effect. Consumer-tech growth teams adopted the same logic through the 2010s, as cohort-and-funnel tools such as Mixpanel and Amplitude made it cheap to slice retention by signup channel, and it became a standard growth-team habit rather than a named academic method. The sentence Aditi could say in the boardroom without sounding glib was: "Before we decide what to fix, we need to know whether the drop is who we brought in, whether they ever got going, or whether they kept coming back — because each has a different fix."

3. How it actually works

The first step, often skipped, is choosing the segmentation dimension before looking at the answer — acquisition channel, city tier, device, or signup plan — because whichever dimension is picked determines what the decomposition can and cannot see. Aditi chose channel, since Manthan's May-to-August period included a deliberate shift in ad spend ahead of the festival season.

Next, both cohorts are split into the same channel segments, and the segment-level retention rate is computed for each period separately, alongside each segment's share of total signups. This produces two small tables rather than two single numbers. The decomposition then asks a counterfactual question: if the August cohort's channel mix had instead been May's channel mix, but every channel had kept its own May-level retention rate, what would August's blended retention have been? That reweighted number is the mix-adjusted figure, and the gap between it and the true May number is the mix effect — the part of the change explained purely by who signed up, with nothing about the product changing at all.

Whatever gap remains between the mix-adjusted figure and the actual August number is the within-segment effect: a genuine change in how a channel's own users behaved. That remaining effect is then split a second time, within whichever channel moved, into an activation rate (the share of new users who ever cross a first-use milestone, such as completing a first workout within seven days) and a conditional retention rate among those who did activate. Because activation rate multiplied by conditional retention equals the segment's overall retention, this last split is exact arithmetic, not another approximation. Practitioners often stop after the mix step, which is the single most common shortcut that later embarrasses them.

4. Working Manthan's numbers

Aditi pulled the May cohort of 10,000 signups, split by channel: organic and word-of-mouth, referral, and paid social. Table 1 shows both periods.

ChannelMay signupsMay retentionAug signupsAug retention
Organic6,000 (60%)42%5,600 (40%)42%
Referral2,000 (20%)48%1,400 (10%)48%
Paid social2,000 (20%)18%7,000 (50%)12%
Blended10,00038.4%14,00027.6%

The blended row is the arithmetic everyone sees: (6,000×0.42 + 2,000×0.48 + 2,000×0.18) ÷ 10,000 = 3,840 ÷ 10,000 = 38.4 percent in May; (5,600×0.42 + 1,400×0.48 + 7,000×0.12) ÷ 14,000 = 4,284 ÷ 14,000 = 27.6 percent in August, a fall of 10.8 points. Now the counterfactual: apply August's mix (40/10/50) to May's own retention rates (42/48/18) — that is, ask what August would have looked like if only the mix had shifted and each channel had kept behaving exactly as it did in May, including paid social still converting at 18 percent rather than its actual 12. That gives 5,600×0.42 + 1,400×0.48 + 7,000×0.18 = 2,352 + 672 + 1,260 = 4,284, divided by 14,000, which is 30.6 percent. So the mix-adjusted figure is 30.6 percent: mix shift alone, with the product held constant, would have taken retention from 38.4 to 30.6, a 7.8-point fall, simply because paid social — Manthan's weakest-retaining channel — went from a fifth of signups to half of them.

The remaining gap, 30.6 minus the actual 27.6, is 3.0 points, and it lives entirely inside paid social, whose own retention fell from 18 to 12 percent while organic and referral held steady. That is the within-segment effect, and it is the only part of the 10.8-point story that says anything happened to the product experience rather than to the advertising mix.

A second pass: what if paid social hadn't changed at all?

If paid social's retention had stayed at 18 percent, August's blended retention would have been the mix-adjusted 30.6 percent, not 27.6. The entire extra 3-point shortfall Aditi actually observed is attributable to something that happened specifically to paid-social users between May and August — and that something turned out, on inspection, to be an Android push-notification permission prompt that a July release had accidentally moved behind an extra tap, a screen paid-social users saw disproportionately because their onboarding funnel routed through a different landing flow.

Aditi split paid social's own 18-to-12 fall the same exact way, using activation (completing a first workout within seven days) times conditional retention among activated users. Figure 1 shows the two 100-cell grids, each cell one percentage point of the segment's whole population, shaded to the segment's overall retention rate.

Both numbers moved: fewer paid-social users ever completed a first workout, and even the ones who did were slightly less likely to stick around. The activation collapse pointed straight at the delayed push-notification prompt; the smaller conditional-retention slide was consistent with a lower-intent audience reached by the newer, broader ad creative. Two different fixes, one number.

5. What a learner must get right

Mix decomposition is not unique

Segmenting by channel explained the story cleanly; segmenting by city tier or by device might have explained a different-sized share of the same 10.8-point fall, because real populations overlap across dimensions. The decomposition answers "how much does this particular cut explain," not "the" answer.

The order of operations quietly changes the split

Computing the mix effect first, then the within effect, can give a slightly different split than doing it in the reverse order, because of a cross-term where both changed at once. Careful practitioners either report both orderings or average them, rather than presenting one order as the unique truth.

Correlation with a channel is not a causal mechanism

Paid-social users may retain worse partly because the channel selects lower-intent people, not because anything the channel itself does causes churn. The decomposition says where the effect sits; it does not, by itself, explain why that segment behaves as it does.

The activation milestone has to be validated, not assumed

If "first workout in seven days" turns out to be a weak predictor of month-2 retention, the activation/engagement split built on it will mislead. The milestone needs its own check against later retention before it is trusted as a diagnostic.

Cohorts must be compared at equal maturity

Comparing a fully-matured May cohort's month-2 number to an August cohort read too early, before it has had two full months to develop, silently understates August and manufactures a fake decline.

Small segments produce noisy splits

Referral's 1,400 August users is a small enough base that its 48 percent retention rate carries real sampling uncertainty; a decomposition run on such a segment should carry a confidence interval, not a bare point estimate.

It locates the problem; it does not diagnose the mechanism

Once the decomposition says "activation, in paid social," the actual cause — the delayed permission prompt — still has to be found the way any bug is found: reading release notes, watching session replays, talking to support. The decomposition narrows the search; it does not finish it.

A mix effect is not automatically "nothing to worry about"

Even when a drop is entirely explained by mix, that mix may itself be the wrong strategic choice — bringing in cheaper, lower-retaining users on purpose is a decision leadership should make deliberately, not one to wave away because "the product is fine."

6. Where the shape changes

In a consumer app like Manthan, cohorts are large and weekly, and mix shifts are usually driven by marketing seasonality — a festival push, a new city launch. In B2B software, the unit is the account rather than the person, mix means industry vertical or deal size rather than ad channel, activation means time to a first meaningful action such as inviting teammates or generating a first report, and cohorts are small enough that the decomposition is often done quarterly with wider confidence bands rather than weekly. In a marketplace, both sides need separate decompositions — supply and demand — and a demand-side user's engagement can fall for a reason entirely outside that user's own behaviour, namely thinner supply in their city, which blurs activation and engagement in a way a single-sided consumer product never has to untangle. Company stage matters too: an early-stage team with a few hundred signups a month should treat any decomposition as directional and pair it with actual user conversations, while a company at Manthan's scale has enough volume to trust the arithmetic and to make it a standing, weekly-reviewed growth artefact rather than a one-off investigation.

7. Where this goes wrong

Symptom: leadership orders an onboarding redesign the day retention drops. Underlying error: assuming a blended number automatically means a product regression. Cheap diagnostic: run the mix-adjusted counterfactual first; it costs an afternoon of re-weighting existing data before anyone touches the product.

Symptom: a team declares "an activation problem" the same week a new app version shipped. Underlying error: mistaking a change in event logging for a change in behaviour. Cheap diagnostic: check event volumes and app-version distribution before trusting the metric.

Symptom: this month's cohort looks worse than last month's on the same day-30 chart. Underlying error: comparing cohorts at different observation maturity. Cheap diagnostic: only compare cohorts with identical elapsed time since signup.

Symptom: the team shrugs once "it's just mix" is confirmed. Underlying error: treating "not a product bug" as equivalent to "not a problem." Cheap diagnostic: ask explicitly whether the new mix is one the company chose on purpose.

8. What good looks like

By the Friday before the board meeting, Aditi's slide showed three numbers instead of one: the actual 10.8-point fall, the 7.8 points explained by the shift toward paid social, and the 3.0 points explained by that channel's own activation problem. She recommended fixing the notification-prompt regression immediately, since it was cheap and unambiguous; tightening paid-social targeting toward higher-intent creative over the next quarter, since the mix question was a strategic one for the marketing lead rather than hers alone to solve; and adding channel-level retention as a standing line on the weekly growth dashboard, so no future drop would arrive as a single frightening number again.

9. The decision, and two questions

Aditi told the board that Manthan's product had not broadly regressed, that a specific, fixed bug explained the sharper part of the decline, and that the rest reflected a deliberate and reversible marketing choice. The board approved both the engineering fix and a narrower paid-social targeting test rather than a broad product freeze. Her own next step was to study root-cause analysis of a metric change in more depth, because decomposition had told her precisely where to look but not, on its own, why the notification prompt had moved in the first place.

Two questions worth sitting with: if you had seen only the blended 38-to-28 number, what would you have decided, and would it have been wrong? And which segmentation dimension would you have reached for first at your own company, and why that one rather than another equally plausible cut?
